title: MORE Thermal Gauge Theories at Finite $θ$ and $μ$ from Real-Time Quantum Simulation
abstract: Imaginary-time evolution can be reconstructed from real-time quantum simulations using exact integral transforms. We identify the construction of Guo, Shibu, Lin, and Zhao as a continuous linear combination of Hamiltonian simulations and show that its slow $1/t_{\rm cut}$ convergence arises from a redundant kernel component. We extend the construction from pure-state matrix elements to thermal traces and correlators. One real-time dataset then reconstructs targeted inverse temperatures, Euclidean separations, and chemical potentials through classical post-processing, bringing finite-$(T,θ,μ)$ physics within reach of real-time quantum simulation without thermal-state preparation. We benchmark the method on one- and two-flavor lattice Schwinger models, including circuit-level simulations with depolarizing noise.
summary: This paper introduces a novel methodology to calculate thermal properties of quantum field theories, such as those found in lattice gauge theories, using only real-time quantum simulation data. By employing exact integral transforms and optimizing the reconstruction kernel, the authors enable the extraction of finite-temperature, finite-$	heta$, and finite-$\mu$ physics from a single set of measurements. This significantly advances the feasibility of simulating complex thermal states on quantum hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is reconstructing imaginary-time evolution (needed for thermal factors and Euclidean correlators) from real-time quantum simulations, especially for finite temperature, topological angle, and chemical potential.
main_result: The authors developed a method that allows a single real-time dataset to reconstruct targeted thermal physics parameters ($ eta, 	au, \mu$) through classical post-processing, circumventing the need for explicit thermal state preparation.
method: The technique uses exact integral transforms to map real-time quantum measurements onto imaginary-time evolution operators, optimizing the reconstruction kernel for faster convergence.
model_or_system: The method is benchmarked on lattice Schwinger models (one- and two-flavor) within the context of lattice field theory, allowing the study of thermal properties in gauge theories.
key_observables: Partition functions, thermal traces, Euclidean correlators, topological charge ($\langle Q angle$), and chiral condensate ($\langle  ar{\psi}\psi angle$).
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), imaginary-time interval ($	au$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and topological angle ($	heta$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on the existence of an exact integral transform relating real-time and imaginary-time evolution, and it requires classical post-processing to extract the final physical quantities.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three-step pipeline: quantum measurement, single data acquisition, and classical reconstruction. Figure 2 compares the convergence rates of different reconstruction kernels, showing superior performance for the near-optimal kernel. Figure 3 compares two circuit implementations for the required measurements.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the mathematical identity for reconstruction, then extends this from pure states to thermal traces and correlators. It details the optimization of the reconstruction kernel, presents the full pipeline using the Schwinger model, and finally discusses error budgeting and observable extraction.
why_interesting: The technique provides a powerful, resource-efficient bridge between real-time quantum simulation (a major focus in quantum computing) and equilibrium statistical mechanics calculations, which is highly relevant for studying thermalization and phase transitions in quantum systems.
